archetype.name: Title Contender (rim-protection first)
archetype.definition: A team whose margin, not just its record, sits among the league's best, built on a dominant center, an elite defensive interior and a deep guard rotation, with last season's top-ranked finish behind it.

report.headline: The 62-win Spurs are back, and the margin says the 8-2 start is real.
report.take:
San Antonio arrives as the defending top team on the site: 62-20 last season, ranked first, 13 playoff wins. Ten games into 2026-27 it looks like the same machine. A Net Rtg of 10.3 ranks third in the league, the offense sits sixth by ORtg (118) and the defense fourth by DRtg (107.7). W vs Pt Diff is exactly 0, so the 8-2 record is what the margin implies, not a run of coin flips. The two losses came in the first two games, at home to OKC and Houston. The 8-game winning streak since has been fueled by blowouts more than escapes: only the 112-111 win over Dallas and the overtime win at Utah were close.

The engine is Victor Wembanyama. He is first among 91 centers on the site, with a 14.4 BPM at a 36.2 USG % and a team-best +41.5 On-Off. His fingerprints are all over the defense: opponents shoot 59.4% at the rim, second-best in the league and 5.8 points under the league average. The defensive rebounding (75.6 DRB %, fourth) finishes possessions. On offense the Spurs are not a shooting team. Their eFG % of 52.4 ranks 20th and they take fewer threes than most (3PA Rate 23rd). They win the possession game instead, with the league's lowest TOV % (11.3), a top-10 FT Rate and the third-most rebounds a game.

The grades show how lopsided the roster is. The backcourt is an A+. Fox (64.4 TS %, +29.2 On-Off) and Harper (+25 On-Off) have been the best of a four-guard rotation, while Castle carries real usage (24.6 USG %) at a poor 50.5 TS %. The frontcourt, though, grades D- even with the league's best center in it, because everyone else is underwater. Keldon Johnson has a -2.5 BPM and the backup center minutes have been brutal, with Kornet at a -36.2 On-Off. Translation: the Spurs are elite with Wembanyama on the floor and ordinary without him. That is the real fragility here, more than anything in the record.

What the numbers flatter is mostly the schedule. Beyond the two early losses, the wins have come against Sacramento, Utah twice, Portland, Dallas and Minnesota. That is not a gauntlet. Opponents are also shooting 36.8% from three (23rd), worse than last season's 35.2%. With an interior this strong, that is likely part noise and part the price of packing the paint. The 66-win pace is too rich, but a team this efficient on both ends with last year's résumé is a legitimate title favorite, not a hot start.

strengths.title: Wembanyama's rim wall
strengths.body: Opponents shoot 59.4% at the rim, second in the league and well below the 65.2% league norm, and they get there less often than average too. That is the core of a top-4 defense. It mirrors last season's top-3 unit, so it is structural, not a small-sample blip.

strengths.title: Winning the possession battle
strengths.body: The Spurs have the league's lowest TOV % and finish defense with a top-4 DRB %, which leads to the third-most rebounds a game. That lets an offense with only middling shooting still rank sixth. Ball security was a strength last season too (11.8 TOV %), so this should hold.

strengths.title: Deep, efficient guard rotation
strengths.body: Four guards play big minutes and the group grades A+. Fox (64.4 TS %) and Harper (+25 On-Off) lead the way, and Champagnie supplies spacing on the wing at a 67.6 TS %. The depth also means one guard's absence, like Vassell's day-to-day status, barely dents the rotation.

concerns.title: Cliff when Wembanyama sits
concerns.body: The frontcourt grades D- despite housing the league's top-ranked center, because the bigs around him are losing their minutes. Kornet's -36.2 On-Off and Johnson's -2.5 BPM show how much the bench minutes at the four and five cost. This is the one area where the team's ceiling depends on a single player's health and workload.

concerns.title: Leaky three-point defense
concerns.body: Opponents are hitting 36.8% from three, 23rd in the league and above the 34.8% league average. Some of that is variance ten games in, and some is the trade-off of walling off the paint. Golden State's league-best shooting this week is a real test of it.

concerns.title: Shooting has slipped from last year
concerns.body: The eFG % of 52.4 ranks 20th, down from 55.9 last season, and Castle is using a quarter of the possessions at a 50.5 TS %. The offense is still sixth because of turnovers and rebounding, but its efficiency ceiling is lower than last year's fourth-ranked unit.

trend.note: An 0-2 start at home gave way to 8 straight wins. The last five, all wins, came by 14 points a game, 3.7 better than the season rate, though against mostly soft opposition.

weekAhead.headline: Three bottom-tier opponents and one real test against Golden State
weekAhead.body:
Three of the four games come against teams ranked 25th, 30th and 27th on the site, and all three are on the road. Phoenix and Chicago are two of the league's worst defenses by DRtg and two of its weakest defensive rebounding teams. That plays straight into a Spurs team that lives on the glass and at the rim. Chicago also lets opponents take the highest share of their shots at the rim of any team, which is an open invitation for Wembanyama. Utah has the league's 29th-ranked offense and offers little resistance.

The game that matters is Golden State at home. The Warriors are 7-3, rank fifth by ORtg and shoot a league-best 39.5% from three while taking a lot of them. That points directly at the Spurs' one soft spot, perimeter defense. On the other end, Golden State's rim defense ranks 29th, so Wembanyama should eat inside. Anything less than three wins would be a disappointment; a 4-0 week is the expectation.

keyMatchups.title: Warriors' shooting vs Spurs' perimeter
keyMatchups.body: Golden State leads the league in 3P % and ranks sixth in 3PA Rate, while San Antonio's opponents shoot 36.8% from deep. If the Spurs can't run the Warriors off the line, this is the game the streak ends.

keyMatchups.title: Wembanyama at the Warriors' rim
keyMatchups.body: Golden State allows 71.2% at the rim, 29th in the league, though it limits how often opponents get there. With a frontcourt graded D-, the Warriors have no obvious answer for a center with a 14.4 BPM.

keyMatchups.title: Glass mismatch in Phoenix, Chicago
keyMatchups.body: Phoenix ranks last in DRB % and Chicago 29th, against a Spurs team that is 13th in offensive rebounding and third in RPG. Second chances should turn these road games into comfortable margins.

weekAhead.watch: How the Spurs defend Golden State's three-point volume on Nov. 13, the first true test of the perimeter defense since the opening-week losses.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable. A top-4 defense keyed by elite rim protection, the league's best ball security and strong rebounding are the same traits that produced last season's 62 wins and top-3 Net Rtg. With W vs Pt Diff at 0, there is no close-game luck to give back. The 66-win pace will cool as the schedule toughens and the margin settles. Still, a Net Rtg in the high single digits and something near last season's win total is the reasonable expectation.

On regression, opponents' three-point shooting should drift back toward average, helping the defense. The 52.4 eFG % has room to climb toward last year's level if Castle's efficiency improves. The downside risk is concentrated in one place. The team falls apart when Wembanyama sits, so his availability is the single biggest variable for both the seed and a deep playoff run.

confidence.note: Only 10 games against a soft slate, but the profile matches last season's 62-win team.
